input.title: The Tuesday Barrel
input.premise: A dock hand sits grey-faced on the pavement at the Sluice Grub stall after a cheap cup from somebody else's barrel. Dessa Vey keeps ladling clean water at two a cup, and the only way the next cheap cup stops is if she says where hers comes from, which is the one thing that stops her barrel too.

input.persona: Warm and fast, a price in every sentence. Wants her regulars fed and her stall open; fears the day the barrel stops coming; would never overcharge a child. Goes thin and quiet when a question costs more than a cup.

input.name: where the barrel comes from
input.description: What Dessa has decided not to ask about and finally says aloud: her clean barrel comes stamped from Weir Exchange every Tuesday. To her it means the stall she keeps open runs on somebody else's missing water.

input.title: The Cheap Cup
input.summary: What a bad cup does on a Sump Row pavement, and what it costs Dessa to say where the good ones come from. Once it is over, the street's clean water has an address.

input.title: Poured Free
input.epilogue: Dessa tells you, quietly, that the barrel comes stamped from Weir Exchange every Tuesday. Then she pours the dock hand a cup of hers and does not charge him for it.

narrative.description: At the Sluice Grub stall a dock hand sits on the wet pavement with his back to the counter, grey in the face, a stranger kneeling beside him with two fingers on his wrist.
narrative.playerHint: Go to the Sluice Grub stall.
narrative.stake: Dessa wants someone to see what a one-coin cup does before the queue closes over him; if nobody sees, the next cheap cup is somebody's child.

narrative.description: Dessa keeps ladling while the queue watches the man on the pavement, and waits for you to ask the question she has priced out of reach.
narrative.playerHint: Talk to Dessa Vey at Sluice Grub.
narrative.stake: Telling means the barrel stops; not telling means the cheap barrels win. Either way the street pays.

dialogue.opening: Cup's two, bowl's three. His was one, two stalls down, and you get what one buys. Mine's clean. Don't look at me like that.

choices.text: Why is yours clean when nobody's ration is?
choices.reply: Because I pay for clean. Questions cost extra, love, and I'm all out.

choices.text: Tell me where the barrel comes from, and the cheap ones stop too.
choices.reply: [sigh] Weir Exchange. Stamped, every Tuesday, same seal as the clinic's. There. Now pour him one of mine, go on. That one's free.

input.description: A dock hand sits on the wet pavement in front of the Sluice Grub stall, grey in the face, a stranger kneeling beside him with two fingers on his wrist.
